tldr: To fast-track simulations of force transfer between exoskeletons and human soft tissue, this paper benchmarks the accuracy of MuJoCo's deformable model feature (flexcomp) against a finite element model (COMSOL). While MuJoCo captures overall force trends well, it reveals key limitations: excessive stiffening caused by element volumetric locking, severe underestimation of viscoelastic damping (hysteresis), and significant computational slowdowns as contact points multiply.
hero_caption: The three benchmark cases examined in this study. From left to right: (a) local indentation with a spherical indenter, (b) uniform compression with a flat plate, and (c) flat-plate compression of a thigh cylinder model mimicking bone and soft tissue. Complexity increases step-by-step from simple localized deformation to an exoskeleton-like structure to compare MuJoCo and COMSOL.
overview:
When an exoskeleton assists human movement, not all actuator force reaches the skeleton. Soft tissues like skin, subcutaneous fat, and muscle act like cushions—absorbing, dissipating, and delaying the release of energy, which leads to power loss and poor fit. Simulating these dynamics is essential. However, conventional musculoskeletal models often treat human segments as rigid bodies, whereas high-fidelity finite element method (FEM) software is computationally too expensive to embed inside whole-body motion simulation loops.

To bridge this gap, the authors turned to MuJoCo, a physics engine widely used in robotics. MuJoCo recently introduced "flexcomp," a feature that models deformable bodies using linear finite elements. This allows coupled multibody dynamics and soft-tissue deformation to run within a single framework. But how reliable is this simplified FEM approach from a biomechanical standpoint? Until now, no benchmarks existed comparing it directly against rigorous FEM.

In this work, the authors set up three test cases using tissue-mimicking silicone: spherical indentation, block compression, and thigh-model compression. They directly compared two of MuJoCo's hyperelastic formulations (StVK and SNH models) against COMSOL's nonlinear FEM (Yeoh model with a generalized Maxwell viscoelastic model). While force trends matched closely with correlations of 0.97 to 0.99, MuJoCo exhibited a much stiffer response due to volumetric locking and severely underestimated energy dissipation (hysteresis). Furthermore, as the number of contact points grew, MuJoCo's computational speed dropped sharply, in some cases running slower than COMSOL.
contributions: Providing the first quantitative evaluation of MuJoCo's deformable body feature (flexcomp) for mechanics and strain energy against high-fidelity FEM software (COMSOL).
Constructing three benchmark test cases of increasing complexity, ranging from simple spherical indentation to an idealized cylindrical thigh model.

Pinpointing the physical mechanisms behind MuJoCo's limitations: volumetric locking in linear tetrahedral elements (causing excessive stiffening in nearly incompressible materials) and the inability of Rayleigh damping to capture viscoelastic hysteresis.
Uncovering the computational bottleneck in MuJoCo's discrete contact formulation when degrees of freedom and contact points scale up.

sections.heading: How should we model the gap between exoskeletons and humans?
sections.summary: Evaluating exoskeleton assistance efficiency requires modeling the deformation and dynamics of soft tissue between the cuffs and the bone. This section introduces why MuJoCo—which handles both multibody dynamics and deformable bodies—was benchmarked against the high-fidelity FEM tool COMSOL.
sections.details:
Exoskeletons transmit forces to the human body through straps and cuffs. Before reaching the skeleton, however, forces must pass through viscoelastic soft tissues such as skin, fat, and muscle. Previous studies have pointed out that this soft tissue temporarily absorbs assistance energy and releases it with a time delay, resulting in reduced efficiency.

Because measuring interface stresses and power losses in human experiments is challenging, simulations are essential. Yet most existing exoskeleton models either assume the human body is rigid or treat the interface as an idealized torque source, rarely incorporating soft-tissue dynamics explicitly.

While FEM is the gold standard for soft-tissue deformation analysis, dedicated FEM tools like COMSOL or Ansys carry heavy computational loads, making them difficult to integrate with whole-body musculoskeletal models and robot control loops. On the other hand, the physics engine MuJoCo, favored in robotics and reinforcement learning, offers exceptional contact stability and supports OpenSim-derived musculoskeletal models. With its "flexcomp" library, deformable bodies can now also be modeled via linear FEM.

The authors previously modeled a thigh-exoskeleton interface using flexcomp, but observed discrepancies with experimental data without knowing whether the limits came from the model itself. Thus, this study benchmarks MuJoCo's deformable models against COMSOL as ground truth to evaluate how accurately it captures soft-tissue deformation and energy dissipation.

sections.heading: Three benchmark cases and simulation setup: MuJoCo vs COMSOL
sections.summary: Using silicone elastomer (Ecoflex 00-10) as a tissue surrogate, the authors set up three cases: localized indentation, uniform compression, and a thigh model. They detail the setup of MuJoCo's two elasticity models, COMSOL's hyperelastic-viscoelastic model, and the evaluation metrics.
sections.details:
### II-A Three Validation Cases
To mimic biological soft tissue, the authors used Ecoflex 00-10 silicone (density $1040\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$), which reproduces the compressive response of a human thigh. Validation was conducted across three stages:
- Case 1 (Spherical Indentation): A rigid sphere of radius $10\,\mathrm{mm}$ was indented up to a depth of $9\,\mathrm{mm}$ into a $70\times 70\times 25\,\mathrm{mm}$ block to evaluate localized large-strain behavior.
- Case 2 (Compression): The same block was uniformly compressed up to a depth of $5\,\mathrm{mm}$ using a flat rigid plate.
- Case 3 (Compression of a Thigh): A soft-tissue cylinder of outer diameter $90\,\mathrm{mm}$ bonded to a rigid bone of diameter $15\,\mathrm{mm}$ was compressed up to a depth of $10\,\mathrm{mm}$ with a flat plate.

### II-B MuJoCo Modeling Setup
Using MuJoCo 4.0.0's flexcomp, geometries were meshed with linear tetrahedral elements. Material parameters were set to Young's modulus $E = 40\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and Poisson's ratio $\nu = 0.485$ (nearly incompressible), with stiffness-proportional Rayleigh damping (coefficient $0.002\,\mathrm{s}$). Two elasticity models were evaluated: the Saint Venant-Kirchhoff (StVK) model, which computes strain energy from the deformation gradient, and the Stable Neo-Hookean (SNH) model, which accounts for volumetric changes. Contacts were resolved as discrete point contacts, solved with a Newton solver at a $2\,\mathrm{ms}$ timestep for numerical stability.

### II-C COMSOL Reference Model
Simulations in COMSOL Multiphysics 6.2 used the Solid Mechanics interface. A three-term Yeoh hyperelastic model captured nonlinear elasticity, combined with a two-branch generalized Maxwell viscoelastic model (Prony series) to represent rate-dependent energy loss. A mixed displacement-pressure formulation prevented numerical locking from incompressibility, and continuous penalty-based contact with Coulomb friction (friction coefficient 0.5) was applied at the boundaries.

### II-D Data Collection and Metrics
Reaction force $F$ and strain energy $U$ were recorded as functions of indentation depth $d$. In addition, the hysteresis ratio $\eta = (E_{\mathrm{load}} - E_{\mathrm{unload}}) / E_{\mathrm{load}}$ was calculated from the mechanical work during loading and unloading cycles, and computational speed was evaluated using the Real-Time Factor (RTF), the ratio of computation time to real time.

captions.F2: Simulation behavior in MuJoCo (top) and COMSOL (bottom) at initial contact (left) and maximum indentation depth (right). MuJoCo shows numerous discrete contact points and normal force vectors, whereas COMSOL visualizes continuous von Mises stress distributions.

sections.heading: Force and energy comparisons: Overly stiff responses and missing damping
sections.summary: Although force-displacement curves showed high overall correlation (0.97–0.99), MuJoCo exhibited a noticeably stiffer reaction force than COMSOL. Furthermore, hysteresis was only 10–20% of COMSOL's value, and MuJoCo lost its computational speed advantage in cases with many contact points.
sections.details:
### Force and Strain Energy Responses
Looking at the force-displacement curves (Fig. F3, top), MuJoCo's StVK and SNH models correlated strongly with COMSOL's Yeoh model (Pearson correlation $r = 0.97\sim 0.99$), capturing the overall qualitative trends. However, substantial deviations appeared in absolute values:
- In Case 1 (local indentation), MuJoCo's force rose more steeply than COMSOL's, showing a stiffer response. The root mean square error (RMSE) was $0.8\,\mathrm{N}$ for StVK and $3.6\,\mathrm{N}$ for SNH. Additionally, the StVK model exhibited a sudden force drop of about $0.16\,\mathrm{N}$ near an indentation depth of $8.55\,\mathrm{mm}$.
- In Case 2 (flat compression), StVK force matched COMSOL relatively well (RMSE $1.8\,\mathrm{N}$), though strain energy differed. The SNH model stiffened excessively as compression increased, reaching an RMSE of $13\,\mathrm{N}$.
- In Case 3 (thigh model), the discrepancy was largest: RMSE reached $39.4\,\mathrm{N}$ for StVK and $53.6\,\mathrm{N}$ for SNH, with MuJoCo's peak force spiking to more than double COMSOL's.

### Severe Underestimation of Hysteresis (Energy Dissipation)
Comparing hysteresis ratios during loading and unloading (Table III), COMSOL showed $7.67\%\sim 15.90\%$ energy dissipation from viscoelasticity. In contrast, MuJoCo's StVK model dissipated only $1.81\%\sim 3.73\%$ (12–24% of COMSOL), and the SNH model dissipated just $0.34\%\sim 1.77\%$ (4–11% of COMSOL). MuJoCo converted 89–98% of mechanical work directly into recoverable elastic strain energy, failing to capture the dissipative cushioning characteristic of real soft tissue.

### Computational Speed Reversal
Comparing the Real-Time Factor (RTF) across simulations (Table IV), MuJoCo was 2 to 2.5 times faster than COMSOL in Case 1. However, in Case 2, where contact surface expanded and degrees of freedom grew, MuJoCo became about 3 times slower. In Case 3, MuJoCo was unexpectedly roughly 16 times slower than COMSOL.

captions.F3: Contact force (top) and strain energy (bottom) versus indentation depth for the three cases. Solid lines represent COMSOL, dashed lines MuJoCo StVK, and dotted lines MuJoCo SNH. MuJoCo models exhibit steeper force and energy rises than COMSOL, with the largest divergence occurring in Case 3 (thigh model).

sections.heading: Why does the gap occur? Insights for robotics simulation
sections.summary: MuJoCo's excessive stiffening stems from volumetric locking in first-order tetrahedral elements, while its missing hysteresis is due to Rayleigh damping being an inadequate substitute for true viscoelasticity. A rapid explosion in discrete contact points also spikes solver burden, offering practical takeaways for exoskeleton interface modeling.
sections.details:
### Why Does MuJoCo Stiffen Excessively?
The primary culprit is "volumetric locking." When simulating nearly incompressible materials ($\nu \approx 0.5$) with low-order linear finite elements (first-order tetrahedra), element volume constraints over-constrain the system, artificially stiffening the entire mesh. COMSOL avoids this using higher-order quadratic elements with a mixed displacement-pressure formulation. MuJoCo's flexcomp, prioritizing computational simplicity, uses linear tetrahedra, which lock up under large compressive strains.

### Limitations of Rayleigh Damping
MuJoCo relies on stiffness-proportional Rayleigh damping ($\mathbf{F} = -c\mathbf{K}\dot{\mathbf{x}}$) to represent viscosity. However, this simplified velocity-dependent force cannot reproduce stress relaxation or frequency-dependent hysteresis (such as in a Generalized Maxwell model). Under quasi-static loading speeds, it dissipates virtually no energy.

### The Mechanism Behind the Slowdown
Contrary to MuJoCo's reputation for high speed, it lagged far behind COMSOL in Cases 2 and 3 due to fundamental contact formulation differences. COMSOL solves continuous penalty contacts across smooth boundary surfaces. MuJoCo, however, treats each surface mesh vertex and element as an independent rigid degree of freedom, generating countless discrete point contacts (Fig. F2). As contact area widens, the constraint count explodes, driving up the cost of Hessian matrix evaluations in the Newton solver and making it slower than continuum FEM.

### Recommendations for Researchers
In its current form, MuJoCo flexcomp cannot match COMSOL's quantitative precision for soft-tissue interfaces. However, it remains valuable for identifying contact force trends and general pressure concentrations. Future work will need higher-order elements, native viscoelastic constitutive models, and careful tuning of mesh density and solver options (such as using the CG solver) to balance fidelity and speed.

takeaways: MuJoCo's flexcomp reliably captures soft-tissue deformation trends (correlation > 0.97), but overestimates reaction forces in nearly incompressible materials due to volumetric locking.
Rayleigh damping alone cannot replicate the viscoelastic energy dissipation (hysteresis) of soft tissue, causing MuJoCo to dramatically underestimate energy loss.
In simulations with broad contact areas, MuJoCo's discrete point contact formulation scales poorly, sometimes running slower than standard FEM tools like COMSOL.
When modeling soft tissues in exoskeleton or grasping simulations, calibrating flexcomp stiffness parameters against experimental data is strongly recommended.
limitations: Validation was limited to homogeneous (single-layer) silicone blocks and a simplified cylinder model, without accounting for anatomical multilayering (skin, fat, fascia) or tissue anisotropy.

Because identical constitutive laws (hyperelastic strain energy functions) could not be matched one-to-one across both engines, element formulation differences and material model differences were evaluated concurrently.
The benchmarks focused strictly on quasi-static indentation rates (1–5 mm/s), without exploring high-velocity dynamic impacts or cyclic loading during fast locomotion.
